editorialDecl.p: EEBO-TCP is a partnership between the Universities of Michigan and Oxford and the publisher ProQuest to create accurately transcribed and encoded texts based on the image sets published by ProQuest via their Early English Books Online (EEBO) database (http://eebo.chadwyck.com). The general aim of EEBO-TCP is to encode one copy (usually the first edition) of every monographic English-language title published between 1473 and 1700 available in EEBO.

EEBO-TCP aimed to produce large quantities of textual data within the usual project restraints of time and funding, and therefore chose to create diplomatic transcriptions (as opposed to critical editions) with light-touch, mainly structural encoding based on the Text Encoding Initiative (http://www.tei-c.org).

The EEBO-TCP project was divided into two phases. The 25,368 texts created during Phase 1 of the project (2000-2009), initially available only to institutions that contributed to their creation, were released into the public domain on 1 January 2015. The approximately 40,000 texts produced during Phase 2 (2009- ), of which 34,963 had been released as of 2020, originally similarly restricted, were similarly freed from all restrictions on 1 August 2020. As of that date anyone is free to take and use these texts for any purpose (modify them, annotate them, distribute them, etc.). But we do respectfully request that due credit and attribution be given to their original source.
Users should be aware of the process of creating the TCP texts, and therefore of any assumptions that can be made about the data.

Text selection was based on the New Cambridge Bibliography of English Literature (NCBEL). If an author (or for an anonymous work, the title) appears in NCBEL, then their works are eligible for inclusion. Selection was intended to range over a wide variety of subject areas, to reflect the true nature of the print record of the period. In general, first editions of a works in English were prioritized, although there are a number of works in other languages, notably Latin and Welsh, included and sometimes a second or later edition of a work was chosen if there was a compelling reason to do so.

Image sets were sent to external keying companies for transcription and basic encoding. Quality assurance was then carried out by editorial teams in Oxford and Michigan. 5% (or 5 pages, whichever is the greater) of each text was proofread for accuracy and those which did not meet QA standards were returned to the keyers to be redone. After proofreading, the encoding was enhanced and/or corrected and characters marked as illegible were corrected where possible up to a limit of 100 instances per text. Any remaining illegibles were encoded as <gap>s. Understanding these processes should make clear that, while the overall quality of TCP data is very good, some errors will remain and some readable characters will be marked as illegible. Users should bear in mind that in all likelihood such instances will never have been looked at by a TCP editor.
The texts were encoded and linked to page images in accordance with level 4 of the TEI in Libraries guidelines.

Copies of the texts have been issued variously as SGML (TCP schema; ASCII text with mnemonic sdata character entities); displayable XML (TCP schema; characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or text strings within braces); or lossless XML (TEI P5, characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or TEI g elements).
Keying and markup guidelines are available at the Text Creation Partnership web site.
This file is the EEBO-TCP transcription with editorial layers added inline; nothing of the transcription has been removed.

choice/orig holds the text as printed; choice/reg holds the modern reading. reg/@resp says who decided it (#auto = machine, #editor = reviewed by hand); reg/@type is spelling, case, punctuation, spacing, grammar (an archaic form modernized: thou, hath, -eth) or emendation (another word, or a word added or removed). Where the editor overrode the machine, the editor's reg comes first and the machine's proposal follows as a second reg[@resp='#auto'].
choice/abbr + choice/expan: macron abbreviations (e.g. frō = from) and superscript contractions (yᵉ = the).
supplied: letters or words lost to illegible print, with @cert and a comment giving the evidence; the TCP gap element is kept inside.

Spelling regularized: u/v, i/j, silent final e, doubled consonants, -ie to -y, -nesse to -ness, and a word list. Grammatical forms (hath, doth, thou, thee, thy, ye, shalt, wilt, art, hast, dost) are retained. Footnote text is left in original spelling.
list[@change='#review']: run-in enumerations (I. ... II. ...) set out as numbered lists; the printed numerals are kept in label.
head[@type='edition']: section title used by this edition; the printed heading is kept in the preceding head. @change='#review' points at the revisionDesc entry for these structural changes.
Line breaks are those of the TCP transcription (newlines in the text; g[@ref='char:EOLhyphen'] marks a word hyphenated at line end). pb/@n is the printed page, pb/@facs the page image.
reg[@type='spacing']: a space this edition adds (empty orig) or removes (empty reg) between words.
@prev/@next link blocks this edition runs together into one paragraph; they stay separate elements as printed.
lg[@rend='paragraphs']: verse this edition sets a line to a paragraph.
item[@rend='paragraph']: a printed list item this edition sets as a paragraph.
list[@rend='inline']: a printed list this edition runs into its sentence.
label[@type='head']: a heading this edition adds (its level in @n); it is not printed text.
@rend='run-on': a block this edition runs on from the one before without a space between them.
list/@rend: the numbering this edition gives a list (a Typst numbering pattern, e.g. 'a)'); item/@n on its first item: the number it starts from.
hi inside reg: words of this edition's reading set in italic.

div.p: THE PriviePrivy Key OF HEAVEN; OR, Twenty Arguments for CLOSET-PRAYER: IN A Select DiſcourſeDiscourse on that Subject: With the reſolutionresolution of ſeveralseveral conſiderableconsiderable QueſtionsQuestions; the main Objections alſoalso againſtagainst CloſetCloset-Prayer, are here anſweredanswered; Cautions propounded, and the Point improved; with ſeveralseveral other things of no ſmallsmall importance, in reſpectrespect of the internal and eternal welfare of the ChriſtianChristian Reader. Twenty ſpecialspecial LeſſonsLessons (in the EpiſtleEpistle Dedicatory to ſomesome afflicted Friends) that we are to learn by that ſeveresevere rod, the PESTILENCE, that now rageth in the midſtmidst of us.
By THOMAS BROOKS, MiniſterMinister of the GoſpelGospel.

O my Dove that art in the clefts of the Rock, in the ſecretsecret places of the ſtairsstairs, let me ſeesee thy countenance, let me hear thy voice, for ſweetsweet is thy voyce, and thy countenance is lovely, Cant. 2. 14.
LONDON, Printed for, and are to be ſoldsold by John Hancock, at the firſtfirst ſhopshop in Popes-head Alley, next to Cornhil. 1665.

div.opener: TO My Worthy and EſteemedEsteemed FRIENDS, Mrs. Elizabeth Drinkwater. Mrs. SuſanSusan Bell. Mrs. Hannah Bourne. Mrs. Mary Taylor. Mrs. Anne White. Mrs. Elizabeth Juxon. Mrs. Rebecah Juxon. Mrs. Mary Baxter. Mrs. Deborah Shepherd. Mrs. Anne Clemons. Mrs. Mary Sionior. Mrs. Anne Snell. Mrs. Anne Ellis. Mrs. Margaret Cutlèr. Mrs. Patience Cartwrigh. Mrs. Mary Shaw. Mrs. Phillip Garret. Mrs. Margaret Winfield. Mrs. Hannah Pippet. Mrs. Mary Chanlor. Mrs. Mary Scot. Mrs. Katherine ƲſherUsher. with their Husbands. &c. All HappineſsHappiness both here, and hereafter: Honoured and Beloved in our Dear Lord JeſusJesus.
div.p:
I HAVE crowded your names together in one EpiſtleEpistle, not from any want of reſpectrespect unto you, for I owe to each of you more
than an EpiſtleEpistle; nor becauſebecause you are in one particular FellowſhipFellowship, for ſoso you are not; but partly becauſebecause the Lord hath made you one with himſelfhimself, in the Son of his love; and partly becauſebecause the Lord at ſeveralseveral times, and in ſeveralseveral wayesways hath exerciſedexercised you all in the Furnace of Affliction; and partly becauſebecause this EpiſtleEpistle may reach you all, and ſpeakspeak to you all, when I cannot, or when I may not, or which is more, when I am not.

Dear Friends, many and great have been the breaches that the Lord hath made upon your perſonspersons, upon your neer and dear Relations, and upon your ſweeteſtsweetest comforts and contentments: There is not one of you but may truly ſaysay with Job, He breaketh me with breach upon breach, Job. 16.
14. God hath chaſtiſedchastised you all round with various Rods; and O that the Lord would help you all to hear the Rod, and him who hath appointed it.
Now that you may, give me leave a little to open and apply to your particulars that
div.q: The Lords voyce cryeth unto the City, and the man of wiſdomwisdom ſhallshall hear thy Name: Hear ye the Rod, and who hath appointed it.
div.p:
The matter that I ſhallshall offer to your conſiderationconsideration from this Scripture, will be not only of ſpecialspecial concernment to your ſelvesselves, but alſoalso of high concernment to all ſortssorts and ranks of men and women, in this ſadsad Day, when the Sword
devours on the one hand, & the PeſtilencePestilence rageth on the other hand.

The Lords voice cryeth unto the City. Tremelius turns it thus, The voice of the Lord doth preach unto this City (for what the matter is, thy Name ſeethseeth) Hear ye the Rod, &c. This City, viz. JeruſalemJerusalem, and ſoso conſequentlyconsequently to all the IſraelitesIsraelites; for in this City all Offices and duties of godlineſsgodliness and humanity were more religiouſlyreligiously performed, or to be performed, than in any other place, becauſebecause of the preſencepresence and majeſtymajesty of God that was amongſtamongst them: But thy MajeſtyMajesty ſeethseeth what wickedneſswickedness is practiſedpractised amongſtamongst them, as is evident in the VerſesVerses following.

Cryeth, The word is from Kara, which ſignifiessignifies, FirſtFirst,
To Cry aloud, or, to make a noiſenoise, IſaIsa. 58. 1. Cry aloud, there is Kara: The word ſignifiessignifies to Cry ſoso loud, as that all may hear, that have ears to hear. Secondly, The word ſignifiessignifies, Openly to proclaim, preach, or publiſhpublish a thing, Exod. 33. 19. I will Proclaim the Name of the Lord before thee: Here is the word Kara. Thirdly, The word ſignifiessignifies, To Cry out, Gen. 39. 15. I lifted up my voyce and cryed: Here is Kara. The Hebrew word 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 hath nine other ſignificationssignifications in Scripture; but becauſebecause they are not pertinent to what is in my eye, I ſhallshall paſspass them by at this time.

And the man of WiſdomWisdom ſhallshall ſeesee thy name. VethuſhiiaVethushiia properly ſignifiessignifies EſſenceEssence; and therefore according to the Hebrew, the words ſhouldshould be
read thus, And the man of EſſenceEssence ſhallshall ſeesee thy Name, &c. thatThat is, he that is a man indeed, he that is not a ſotsot, aſtockastock, a ſtonestone. MoſtMost men are men of folly, and ſoso not worthy of the name of men; but as for ſuchsuch as are truly wiſewise, they ſhallshall ſeesee thy Name. There is a great meaſuremeasure of ſpiritualspiritual Art, of Holy and Heavenly WiſdomeWisdom required, both to enable a man to hear the voice of the Rod, and to underſtandunderstand the language of the Rod: This WiſdomWisdom is too high for a fool, Prov. 24. 7.

Shall ſeesee thy Name. Now the Hebrew word here uſedused 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 may be better derived from JareJar, which ſignifiessignifies to fearefear, than from Raah, that ſignifiessignifies to ſeesee, and ſoso the words will run ſmoothlysmoothly thus, The man of wiſdomwisdom, or of eſſenceessence, ſhallshall fear
thy Name, conſideringconsidering that, 'tis majeſtymajesty it ſelfself that cryeth, and that he is immediately to deal with God himſelfhimself, and not with a poor, weak, mortal worm.

Hear ye the Rod. The word Hear, is from 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
Shamang, which ſignifiessignifies, FirſtFirst, To mark, obſerveobserve, and attend, to what is ſaidsaid, Gen. 29. 33. The Lord hath heard that I was hated; that is, he hath marked it, he hath obſervedobserved it. So here, O mark the Rod, O obſerveobserve the Rod, O attend to what is ſpokenspoken by the Rod. Secondly, The word ſignifiessignifies, to underſtandunderstand what is ſpokenspoken, ſoso Gen. 42. 23. They knew not that JoſephJoseph underſtoodunderstood them: In the Hebrew 'tis, that JoſephJoseph heard them. Now to hear the Rod, is to underſtandunderstand what is ſpokenspoken to us by the Rod. Thirdly,
The word ſignifiessignifies, to believe a thing reported to be true, ſoso Exod. 6. 9. They hearkned not unto MoſesMoses, that is, they did not believe the report that MoſesMoses made. Hear the Rod, that is, believe the report the Rod makes. The Rod reports, that of all evils, Sin is the greateſtgreatest evil; and that of all bitters, Sin is the greateſtgreatest bitter; O believe the report of the Rod. The Rod reports that God is angry, that God is diſpleaſeddispleased; Oh believe its report. The Rod reports the creatures to be meer vanity and vexation of Spirit; O believe its report. The Rod reports our neereſtnearest and deareſtdearest comforts, contentments, and enjoyments to be mixtmixed, mutable, and momentary; O believe its report. The Rod reports Sin to be vile, and the world to be
vain, and Heaven to be glorious, and ChriſtChrist to be moſtmost precious; O believe its report. The Hebrew word hath three other ſignificationssignifications, but being that they are not proper to our purpoſepurpose I ſhallshall paſspass them by.

The Rod. The Hebrew word Matte that is here rendredrendered Rod, hath theſethese three ſignificationssignifications. FirſtFirst, It denotes Power and ſtrengthstrength, PſalPsal. 2. 9. A Rod of Iron. Secondly, It denotes Rigid and harſhharsh Government, IſaIsa. 14. 5. The Lord hath broken the ſtaffestaff, or Rod of the wicked, that is, their rigorous and cruel Government. Nebuchadnezzar ſorelysorely afflicted the Children of Judah, he was a Rod that brake them in pieces, and ruled over them with much rigour in Babilon. Thirdly, It denotes ſoresore afflictions,
and heavy Judgements, PſalPsal. 89. 32. I will viſitvisit your tranſgreſſionstransgressions with a Rod. And thus you are to underſtandunderstand the word Rod in the Text.

And him that hath appointed it. 'Tis'tis God that appoints the Rod, and ordainesordains it for the revenge of the quarrel of his Covenant. The Hebrew word Jegnadah ſignifiessignifies properly to appoint, or conſtituteconstitute. 'Tis'tis God who appoints the Rod, and who conſtitutesconstitutes it to do what ſerviceservice he pleaſethpleaseth. 'Tis'tis God that hath not only a permiſſivepermissive, but alſoalso an active hand, in all the afflictions that come upon his People.
And let thus much ſufficesuffice for the opening of the words.
Now though this choice Garden affords many ſweetsweet Flowers, yet I ſhallshall only preſentpresent you with one, which is this, viz.
div.q: That all the Afflictions, troubles, and tryals, &c. that God layeslays upon his People, are his Rod, and that 'tis their higheſthighest and greateſtgreatest concernment, to hear the voyce of the Rod, and to take out thoſethose LeſſonsLessons that God would have them learn by the Rod.
div.p: For the opening and clearing up of this important Point, I ſhallshall endeavour theſethese two things.
FirſtFirst, To ſhewshow you in what reſpectsrespects Afflictions are like unto a Rod.
Secondly, To ſhewshow you what thoſethose ſpecialspecial LeſſonsLessons are, that you are to learn by the Rod.
For the FirſtFirst, In what reſpectsrespects are afflictions like unto a Rod?
I AnſwerAnswer, In theſethese ſevenseven reſpectsrespects Afflictions are like unto a Rod.

FirſtFirst, The Rod is never made uſeuse of, but when no fair means will prevail with the Child. 'Tis'tis ſoso here, God never takes up the Rod, he never afflicts his People, till he 2 Chron. 36. 15,—ult. Mat. 23. 37, 38. hath tryed all fair wayesways and means to humble them, and reform them: And when none of the offers of grace, the tenders of mercy, the wooings of ChriſtChrist, the ſtrivingsstrivings of the Spirit, northenorth ſmartsmart debates of ConſcienceConscience will awaken them, nor work upon them, then God takes up the Rod, and ſometimessometimes whips them till the blood comes. But,

Secondly, Parents chooſechoose what Rods they pleaſeplease to correct their Children with. The Child ſhallshall not chooſechoose what
Rod he pleaſethpleaseth to be corrected with, O no: 'Tis'tis the prerogative of the Father to chooſechoose the Rod; the Father may chooſechoose and uſeuse either a great Rod or a little Rod, a long Rod or a ſhortshort Rod, a Rod made up of RoſemaryRosemary branches, or a Rod made up of green Birch: 'Tis'tis ſoso here, God chooſethchooseth what Rod, what Affliction he pleaſethpleaseth to exerciſeexercise his people with. You Lev. 26. Deut. 28. Lament. 3. 9,—18. read in the Scripture of very many Rods, but they are all of Gods chooſingchoosing, Amos 3. 6. Is there any evil in the City and hath not the Lord done it? Though there be many Rods to be found in the City, yet there is not one of them, but is of Gods chooſingchoosing, Ruth. 1. 13. It grieveth me much for your ſakessakes, that the hand of the Lord is gone out
againſtagainst me. verſvers. 21. I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me home again empty; why then call ye me Naomi, ſeeingseeing the Lord hath teſtifiedtestified againſtagainst me, and the Almighty hath afflicted me? IſaIsa. 45. 7. I form the light, and create darkneſsdarkness: I make peace and create evil: I the Lord do all theſethese things. Mic. 1. 12. For the inhabitants of Maroth, waited carefully for good; but evil came down from the Lord unto the Gates of JeruſalemJerusalem. David was whipt with many Rods, PſalPsal. 39. 9. Job. 1 but they were all of Gods own chooſingchoosing. And Job was whipt with many Rods, but they were all of Gods own chooſingchoosing. But,

Thirdly, Parents take no pleaſurepleasure, they take no delight to uſeuse the Rod. Every laſhlash the Father gives the
Child, fetches blood from his own heart: The Father corrects the Child, and ſighssighs over the Child; he whips the Child, and at the ſamesame time weeps over the Child. Nothing goes more againſtagainst the Parents heart, nor againſtagainst their hair, than the bringing of their Children under the Rod of Correction; 'Tis'tis ſoso here, Lament. 3. 3. For he doth not afflict willingly (or as the Hebrew runs, he doth not afflict, Millibbo, from his heart) nor grieve the Children of men. You often read, that he delights in mercy; but Mich. 7. 15. where do you once read, that he delights in ſeverityseverity, or in dealing roughly with his People? God very rarely takes 2 Chron. 36. 16. Jer. 5. 19. up the Rod, but when our ſinssins have put a force upon him. 'Tis'tis grievous to God, to
be a grieving his People; 'tis a pain unto him, to be a puniſhingpunishing of them, HoſHos. 11. 8. How ſhallshall I give thee up, Ephraim? howHow ſhallshall I deliver thee, IſraelIsrael? howHow ſhallshall I make thee as Admah? howHow ſhallshall I ſetset thee as Zeboim? Mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together. My JuſticeJustice, ſaithsaith God, calls upon me to rain Hell out of Heaven upon thee, as once I did upon Sodom and Gomorah; but then Mercy interpoſethinterposeth her four ſeveralseveral hows, how, how, how, how, how ſhallshall I give thee up? God puts theſethese four pathetical interrogations to himſelfhimself, becauſebecause none elſeelse in Heaven or Earth could anſweranswer them. The Prophet brings in God ſpeakingspeaking after the manner of men, who being provoked a thouſandthousand thouſandthousand wayesways, by
the vanities and follies of their Children, think to give them up to take their own courſescourses, and to look no more after them; but then their bowels begin to work, and their hearts begin to melt, and they begin to interrogate themſelvesthemselves thus, How ſhallshall we give up theſethese Children? forFor though they be diſobedientdisobedient Children, yet they are Children; how can we turn them out of dooresdoors? howHow can we diſowndisown them? howHow can we diſinheritdisinherit them? forFor though they are rebellious Children, yet they are Children, &c. Afflictions are called Gods work, yea, his ſtrangestrange work; his IſaIsa. 28. 21. act, yea, his ſtrangestrange act, as if God were out of his element, when he is afflicting or chaſtiſingchastising his People. But.

Fourthly, The Rod is ſmartingsmarting, grievous, and troubleſomtroublesom; and ſoso are afflictions to our natures, Heb. 12. 11. Now no chaſteningchastening for the preſentpresent ſeemethseemeth to be joyous but grievous. FleſhFlesh and blood ſtartlesstartles, and is troubled at the leaſtleast trouble. Affliction is a ſortsort of PhyſickPhysick, that makes moſtmost ſicksick. Some write that Tygres will grow mad, and tear their own fleſhflesh, Plutarch lib. de ſuperſtition • superstition•. and rend themſelvesthemselves in pieces, if they do but hear Drums or Tabours ſoundsound about them. Were not Job and Jeremiah Job. 3. Jer. 20. ſuchsuch Tygres, who in the day of their afflictions did more than curſecurse the Day of their birth? O what a bitter cup, what a heavy burden was affliction to them! Job 10. 1. My Soul is weary of my life. Job 7. 15. My Soul chooſethchooseth ſtranglingstrangling and death rather
than life. PſalPsal. 6. 6. I am weary with my groaning. PſalPsal. 69. 1, 2, 3. Save me, O God, for the waters are come in unto my Soul. I ſinksink in deep mire, where there is no ſtandingstanding. I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me. I am weary of my crying, my throat is dryed: mine eyes fail, while I wait for my God. DoubtleſsDoubtless many good men have ſatsat under Elias 1 Kings 19. 4. his Juniper, wiſhingwishing themſelvesthemselves out of the World (if it might ſtandstand with Divine pleaſurepleasure) that they might reſtrest from their ſinssins and ſorrowssorrows, and be rid of their many burdens and bondages, looking upon life little better than a Hell, were it not for the hopes of a Heaven hereafter. But,

Fifthly, When Parents take up the Rod into their hands,
they will not lay it down, till Rodolphus the Emperours Motto was, (Omnia eoe voluntate Dei.) All muſtmust be as God will have it. And this ſhouldshould be every ChriſtiansChristians Motto under the Rod. they have ſubduedsubdued the ſpiritsspirits of their Children, and brought them to ſubmitsubmit and to kiſskiss the Rod, and to ſitsit ſtillstill and quiet before them. 'Tis'tis ſoso here, when God takes up the Rod, he will not lay it down, till he hath brought us to lye quietly at his feet, Lev. 26. 40, 41, 42. If they ſhallshall confeſsconfess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers, with their treſpastrespas, which they have treſpaſſedtrespassed againſtagainst me, and that alſoalso they have walked contrary to me; And that I alſoalso have walked contrary unto them, & brought them into the Land of their enemies; if then their uncircumciſeduncircumcised hearts be humbled, and they then accept of the puniſhmentpunishment of their iniquity, Then Will I remember my Covenant with Jacob, and alſoalso
my Covenant with IſaacIsaac, and alſoalso my Covenant with Abraham will I remember: and I will remember the Land. When God takes up the Rod, his Children muſtmust either bow or break; they muſtmust ſaysay, the Jer. 5. 3, 6. Lord is righteous, they muſtmust kiſskiss the Rod of Correction, or elſeelse deſtructiondestruction will come like a WhirleWhirl-wind upon them.

'Tis'tis reported of the Lyon, that he ſparesspares thoſethose creatures, that fall down before him, and ſubmitsubmit unto him; but as for thoſethose that endeavour to run from him, or to contend with him, thoſethose he tears in pieces. All diſeaſesdiseases and ſickneſſessicknesses are under the command of God, they are all his Sergeants, his ſervantsservants, to execute his pleaſurepleasure: That Mat. 8. 5. isIs an obſervableobservable Text; ChriſtChrist tells the Centurion, that he would come and heal his ſervantservant; the Centurion tells him, that he was not worthy that he ſhouldshould come under his roof, only if he would but ſpeakspeak the word, his ſervantservant ſhouldshould be healed; For (ſaithsaith he verſvers. 9.) I am a man under Authority, having SouldiersSoldiers under me: & I ſaysay to this man go, and he goeth; and to another come, and he cometh; and to my ſervantservant do this and he doth it. Now when JeſusJesus heard this, he marvelled, and ſaidsaid to them that followed, Verily, I ſaysay unto you,
I have not found ſoso great faith, no not in IſraelIsrael, verſvers. 10. But wherein did the greatneſsgreatness of the Centurions faith appear? whyWhy, in this very acknowledgment, that all diſeaſesdiseases were to ChriſtChrist as ſervantsservants, and that they were as much under the command of JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist, as any ſervantservant under heaven is under the command of his MaſterMaster: When ChriſtChrist bids them go and afflict ſuchsuch a man, they go; and torment ſuchsuch a man, they go; and kill ſuchsuch a man, they go; and ſoso when he calls them off, they come off at his call. Dear Friends, it is a very great point of faith to believe theſethese five things.

FirſtFirst, that God is the author of all the diſeaſesdiseases, malladies, and ſickneſſessicknesses, that be in the World, and that he ſetssets them on and call them off at his own
good will and pleaſurepleasure, Amos Lev. 26. Deut. 28. 3. 6. Is there any evil in the City, and hath not the Lord done it? He ſpeaksspeaks of the evil of puniſhmentpunishment, and not of the evil of ſinsin. It was a mad Principle among the Manichees, who refer'd all calamities to the Devil for their author, as if there could be evil in the City, and the Lord have no hand in it.

Secondly, It is a great point of Faith to believe, that all diſeaſesdiseases and ſickneſſessicknesses are limited by God, in reſpectrespect of places. God ſentsent diſeaſesdiseases of all ſortssorts into Egypt, but he forbad them GoſhenGoshen, Exod. 8. 20, 21, 22, 23. Chap. 9, 23, 24, 25, 26. Ponder ſeriouſlyseriously upon theſethese Scriptures. Gods ſhootingshooting his arrows into one Town, and not into another, into one City, and not into another, into
one KingdomeKingdom, and not into another, into one family, & not into another, doth ſufficientlysufficiently evidence, that all diſeaſesdiseases, and ſickneſſessicknesses, are limited by the Holy One of IſraelIsrael, in reſpectrespect of places.

Thirdly, It is a very great point of Faith, to believe that all ſickneſſessicknesses, and diſeaſesdiseases, are limited by God in reſpectrespect of perſonspersons; that they are ſoso, is evident in that PſalPsal. 91. 3,—8. IſaIsa 65. 12. But who lives in the faith of this truth? Sometimes in the ſamesame houſehouse one is infected, and the other is not; ſometimessometimes in the ſamesame bed, the one is ſmittensmitten, and the other is not; ſometimessometimes at the ſamesame table, the one is taken away, and the other is left, &c. and this doth roundly evidence and witneſswitness, that all ſickneſſessicknesses and diſeaſesdiseases are limited by
God in reſpectrespect of perſonspersons, as well as in reſpectrespect of places. But,

Fourthly, It is a great point of Faith, to believe that all diſeaſesdiseases and ſickneſſessicknesses are limited by God in reſpectrespect of the degrees to which they ſhallshall ariſearise. That God that ſetssets bounds to the raging Sea, and that ſaithsaith unto it, Thus far ſhaltshalt thou go, and no further; that God ſetssets bounds to all raging diſeaſesdiseases and ſickneſſessicknesses, and ſaithsaith unto them, thus far you ſhallshall go, and no further: He ſetssets bounds to the Feaver; he ſaithsaith to it, go and ſcorchscorch and burn up ſuchsuch a body ſoso much, and no more; and to the DropſieDropsy, go and drown ſuchsuch a body ſoso much, and no more; and to the raging PeſtilencePestilence, go and weaken ſuchsuch a body ſoso much, and no more; and to the
Stone, go and torment ſuchsuch a body ſoso much, and no more. But,

Fifthly, It is a very great point of Faith, to believe that all diſeaſesdiseases and ſickneſſessicknesses are limited by God, as to their continuance: God ſaithsaith to one diſeaſedisease, go hang upon ſuchsuch a man, ſoso many years; to another, go hang up ſuchsuch a man but a few years; and to another, go hang upon ſuchsuch a man but a year; and to another, go hang upon ſuchsuch a man but a few months; and to another, go hang upon ſuchsuch a man but a few weeks; and to another, go hang upon ſuchsuch a man but a few dayesdays; and to another, go hang upon ſuchsuch a man but a few hours, &c. and accordingly it cometh to paſspass. But,

The eighth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod, (or
by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, to Gal. 5. 24. 1 Cor. 7. 29, 30, 31. Eccl. 1. 2. Prov. 23. 5. Jer. 45. 4, 5 get more weaned, and more mortified affections to all worldly comforts, contentments, and enjoyments. A man never comes to experience ſoso much of the emptineſsemptiness, the nothingneſsnothingness, the uſeleſneſsuselessness, the vanity, the mutability, the impotency, the inſufficiencyinsufficiency, and the uncertainty of all worldly comforts, and enjoyments, as when he comes to fall under the Rod. The conſtantconstant cry of the Rod is, Be dead to the profits, pleaſurespleasures, honours, and applauſesapplauses of the world, be dead to relations, be dead to friends, be dead to every thing below a living JeſusJesus. But,

The ninth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, to get aſſuranceassurance of greater, and better things, than any this
world doth afford. That ſayingsaying Heb. 10. 33, 34. is as true, as it is old, viz. That the aſſuranceassurance of an eternal life, is the life of this temporal life: But having ſpokespoke ſoso much of this particular in my TreatiſeTreatise on AſſuranceAssurance, which is now in your hands, I ſhallshall ſatisfiesatisfy my ſelfself with this hint at preſentpresent. But,

The tenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence,) is, not to deſpiſedespise the Rod, Heb. 12. 5. My Son, deſpiſedespise not thou the chaſteningchastening of the Lord. The Greek Word 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 that is tranſlatedtranslated deſpiſedespise, ſignifiessignifies the littling of a thing: O do not little the Rod, do not leſſenlessen it, do not ſlightslight it, do not make a tuſhtush at it, do not ſetset light by it, do not ſaysay, I will not regard it, he that doth, ſhewsshows himſelfhimself, rather to be a Roman, than
a ChriſtianChristian. Now becauſebecause there is ſuchsuch a deſperatedesperate aptneſsaptness & proneſsproness in many to make light of the Rod, it will be your wiſdomwisdom ſeriouſlyseriously to lay to heart theſethese four particulars.

FirſtFirst, That it is an immediate hand of God; and therefore not to be deſpiſeddespised: 'Tis'tis a Am. 3. 6. Deut. 28. 58, 59, 60, 61. ſadsad and ſinfulsinful thing to deſpiſedespise the mediate hand of God; but 'tis more ſadsad and ſinfulsinful to deſpiſedespise the immediate hand of God. But,

Secondly, 'Tis'tis a mighty hand of God, 1 Pet. 5. 6. Humble your ſelvesselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. Certainly Am. 4. 10. 11. Ez. 38. 22, 23. that heart muſtmust be mightily wicked, that dares deſpiſedespise the mighty hand of God. But,

Thirdly, 'Tis'tis an angry hand of God; and therefore do not deſpiſedespise it, PſalPsal. 90. 7. For we
are conſumedconsumed by thy anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled. VerſVers. 11. Who knoweth the power of thine anger? evenEven according to thy fear, ſoso is thy Num. 16. 46. Ez. 33. 27, 28. 29, Deut 29. 22. 23, 24. 25 wrath. Shall Devils tremble under his angry hand? Yea ſhallshall they roar, as the Sea under his 〈◊〉 wrathful hand, as that Greek word 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . importsImports, in that James 2. 19. And will you preſumepresume to deſpiſedespise his angry hand? theThe Lord forbid. butBut,

Fourthly and laſtlylastly, ConſiderConsider, that it is a holy hand, it is a juſtjust and righteous hand, it is a faithful hand of God; and therefore do not deſpiſedespise it, Jer. 29. 17, 18, 19. Lev. 26. 25. Jer 14. 12, 13, 14. 15. 16 PſalPsal. 119. 75. I know, O Lord, that thy JudgmenttJudgment are right, (or righteouſneſsrighteousness) and that thou in faithfulneſsfaithfulness hast afflicted me. VerſVers. 137. Righteous art thou, O Lord, and upright
are thy Judgments. Certainly none but unholy perſonspersons will be ſoso impudent, as to deſpiſedespise Gods holy hand. Well,

The Eleventh LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence,) is, not to be diſcourageddiscouraged under the Rod, Heb.
• 2. Nor Jer. 27. 13. 2 Sam. 24. 10, 17. faint when thou art rebuked of him. FirſtFirst, It is a Rod in a fathers hand; and therefore do not faint under it. Secondly, God will do much good by the Rod; and therefore do not faint under the Rod. Thirdly, You could not have been without the Rod; and therefore do not faint under the Rod.

Fourthly, The Rod that is now upon, is not according to the greatneſsgreatness of Gods anger, nor according to to the greatneſsgreatness of his power, nor according to the ſtrictneſsstrictness of his JuſticeJustice,
nor according to the demerits of your ſinssins, nor according to the malitious deſiresdesires of Satan, nor according to the deſignesdesigns, plots, and contrivances, of wicked and unreaſonableunreasonable men, nor according to the extenſiveneſsextensiveness of your fears, for you have feared worſeworse things than you feel, nor according to that Rod that hath been upon the Primitive Saints, nor according to that Rod, that many thouſandsthousands of the precious ſonssons and daughters of Zion are under in other parts of the world, and therefore do not faint under the Rod, do not be diſcourageddiscouraged under the Rod.

Fifthly, by fainting under the Rod, you will gratifiegratify Satan, reproach religion, render your ſelvesselves unſerviceableunserviceable, and make work for future Repentance; and therefore do not faint under the Rod. But,

The Twelfth LeſſonLesson that you 2 Chron. 32. 25, 26. Lev. 26. 40, 41, 42. Mic. 7. 9. Lam. 3. 30. Luke 21. 10. are to learn under the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, humbly to kiſskiss the Rod, and patiently & quietly to lye under the Rod, till the Lord ſhallshall either give you a gracious or a glorious deliverance from it. What is the Rod, and what is the raging PeſtilencePestilence, to the horrors of ConſcienceConscience, to the flames of hell, or to an everlaſtingeverlasting ſeparationseparation from the preſencepresence of the Lord, and 2 TheſThes. 1. • 8, 9. from the glory of his power? And therefore put your mouths in the duſtdust, and be ſilentsilent before the Lord. He that hath deſerveddeserved a hanging, if he eſcapeescape with a whipping, hath no cauſecause to murmur or complain; and we that have deſerveddeserved a damning, have little cauſecause to murmur or complain of a whipping, yea, though it ſhouldshould be with a PeſtilentialPestilential-Rod. But,

The thirteenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, highly, fully, freely, and ſignallysignally to juſtifiejustify the Lord, and to think well of the
Lord, & to ſpeakspeak well of the Lord, under the Rod; to that purpoſepurpose conſultconsult theſethese Scriptures, PſalPsal. 119. 75, 137. Neh. 9. 33. Ezr. 9. 13. Lam. 1. 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 4, 15, 18. Dan. 9. 12. 14. 2 Kings 20. 16, 17, 18, 19. Jer. 12. 1, 2. PſalPsal. 129. 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. PſalPsal 22. 1, 2, 3. PſalPsal. 97. 2. But,

The fourteenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, perſonalpersonal reformation. When the Rod ſmartssmarts, & the PeſtilencePestilence rageth, God expects that every man ſhouldshould ſmitesmite upon his thigh, and turn from the evil of his doings, 2 Chron. 7. 13, 14. If I ſhutshut up heaven, that there be no rain, or if I command the locuſtslocusts to devour the Land, or if I ſendsend PeſtilencePestilence among my people: If my people which are called by my name, ſhallshall humble themſelvesthemselves, and pray, & ſeekseek my face, & turn from their wicked wayesways; then will I hear from heaven, & will forgive their ſinsin, & will heal their Land; that is, I will remove the judgments that are upon the Land, & I will confer upon my reforming people all thoſethose favours & bleſſingsblessings that they ſtandstand
in need of. ConſultConsult theſethese Scriptures, Ezr. 10. 14, 19. 2 Chron. 30. 8, 9. And chap. 29. 8, 10, 15, 16. But,

The Fifteenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, to make God your habitation, your ſheltershelter, your refuge. Ponder ſeriouſlyseriously upon theſethese Scriptures, PſalPsal. 91. 2, 9, 10. PſalPsal. 90. 1. PſalPsal. 71. 3. PſalPsal. 57. 1. They dwell moſtmost ſafelysafely, moſtmost ſecurelysecurely, moſtmost nobly, who dwell in God, who live under the ſhadowshadow of the Allmighty, and who every day lodge their ſoulssouls in the boſomebosom of eternal loves. But,

The Sixteenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, to ſetset up God as the great object of your fear, PſalPsal. 119. 119, 120. IſaIsa. 8. 7, 8, 13, 14. comparedCompared. When the Judgments of God are either threatnedthreatened or executed, feared or felt, it highly concerns us to lift up God, as the main object of our fear; we ſhouldshould fear the hand that layeslays on the Rod, more than Job 13. 11. Jer. 36. 24. the Rod it ſelfself. When God takes up
the Rod, when he draws his ſwordsword, and when he ſhootsshoots his PeſtilentialPestilential arrows amongſtamongst us, O how highly doth it concern us to fear before him with a child-like fear, with a reverential fear, with a fear that fortifies the heart againſtagainst ſinsin, and with a fear that fits the Soul for duty, & that draws, yea drives the ſoulsoul to duty. But,

The ſeventeenthseventeenth leſſonlesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, to expect Gods ſingularsingular preſencepresence with you, and his admirable protection over you. ConſultConsult theſethese Scriptures, IſaIsa. 43. 2. Dan. 3. 24, 25. Gen. 39. 39, 40. PſalPsal. 23. 4, 5. PſalPsal. 91. IſaIsa. 63. 9. IſaIsa. 26. 20, 21. Ezek. 9. 4, 6. God is above his people, and beneth them, Deut. 33. 25, 26, 27. He is under them, and over them, Cant. 2. 6. He is before them, & behind them, IſaIsa. 52. 12. & chap. 58. 8. He is on the right hand of his people, and he is on the left hand of his people, PſalPsal. 16. 8. PſalPsal. 121. 5. PſPs. 118. 15, 16 Exod. 14. 22, 29. God is round about his people, PſalPsal. 34. 7.
PſalPsal. 125. 2. And God is in the midſtmidst of his people, Zech. 2. 5. PſalPsal. 46. 5. PſalPsal, 12. 6 O the ſafetysafety, the ſecuritysecurity of the poor people of God, for God is above his people & beneth them, he is under them & over them, he is before them & behind them, he is in the front, & in the rear, and he is round about them, and in the midſtmidst of them. But,

The eighteenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is to live every day in a freſhfresh, choice, & frequent excerciſeexcercise of grace. ConſultConsult theſethese Scriptures, PſalPsal. 91. 2, 3, 4. Jer. 39. 17, 18. Mic. 7. 7, 8, 9. PſalPsal. 40. 1, 2. Hab. 2. 1, 2, 3, 4. Jer. 30. • 1. That man that lives dayly in an exerciſeexercise of grace, that man lives every day in heaven on this ſideside heaven, what-ever affliction or judgment he is under.

The Ninteenth LeſſonLesson that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging PeſtilencePestilence) is, to quicken up your hearts to ſeekseek the Lord by extraordinary wayesways & means, viz. by faſtingfasting & prayer. ConſultConsult theſethese
Scriptures, Num. 16. 46,—ult. PſalPsal. 106. 23, 29, 30. IſaIsa. 22. 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 13. Jon. 3. 5,—ult. 2 Chron. 12. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. 1 Kings 21. 21,—ult. Joel 2. 12, 13, 14, 15. 16, 17. But,

The Twentieth, and ſoso the laſtlast LeſſonLesson, that you are to learn by the Rod (or by the raging peſtilencepestilence) is, To prepare for death, it is to be in actual readineſsreadiness to dye. Ah Friends, every ach, every pain, every diſeaſedisease, is one of deaths warning pieces. There is not a head-ach, not a tooth-ach, not a gripe, not a grief, not a fall, not a wrench, not a plague-ſoresore; but is a divine warning to man, to prepare to die. 'Tis'tis a ſoleemnsoleemn work to die, and therefore we had need prepare to die. 'Tis'tis a work that is to be done but once; and therefore we had need prepare to do that work well, that is to be done but once. In this world, we hear often, & pray often, & read often, and meditate often, & eat often, & drink often, Job 14. 14. Heb. 9. 27. and that which is worſtworst, we ſinsin often; but we muſtmust die but once. Death will try all our graces, & all our experiences, & all our evidences, & all our comforts,
& all our attainments, and all our He that would ſeesee more of this, may read my String of Pearls, and the Funeral Sermon that is at the end of my Book of AſſuranceAssurance.
enjoyments; and therefore we had need to prepare to die. Though there is nothing more certain than death, yet there is nothing more uncertain than, 1. The time when we ſhallshall die. 2. The place where we ſhallshall die. And 3. The manner how we ſhallshall die; as whether we ſhallshall die a ſuddensudden death, or a lingring death, or a violent death; or whether we ſhallshall fall by the ſwordsword abroad, or by famine or peſtilencepestilence at home, or whether we ſhallshall fall by this diſeaſedisease or that; and therefore we had need be alwayesalways in an actual readineſsreadiness to die. No man ſhallshall die the ſoonersooner, but much the eaſiereasier, and the better, for preparing to die: And therefore let us alwayesalways have our loins girt, and our lamps burning. As death leaves us ſoso Judgment will find us; and there fore we have very great cauſecause to ſecuresecure our intereſtinterest in ChriſtChrist, a changed nature, and a pardon in our boſomesbosoms; that ſoso we might have nothing to do, but to die. Except, we prepare to die, all other preparations will
do us no good. In a word, Death is a change, a great change, 'tis the the laſtlast change till the reſurrectionresurrection, 'tis laſtinglasting, yea, an everlaſtingeverlasting change; for it puts a man into an eternalleternal condition of happineſshappiness or miſerymisery; 'tis an univerſaluniversal change, all perſonspersons muſtmust paſspass under this flaming Sword. That Statute Law, DuſtDust thou art, and unto duſtdust thou ſhaltshalt return, will Gen. 3. 18. ſoonersooner or later take hold on all mortals; and therefore it highly concerns us to prepare for death.

And thus I have ſhewnshown you theſethese LeſſonsLessons that you are to learn by the Rod. The Lord grant that your ſoulssouls may fall under thoſethose freſhfresh, thoſethose choice, thoſethose full, and thoſethose conſtantconstant influences and communications of his holy Spirit, as may enable you to take out thoſethose twenty LeſſonsLessons that I have laid open before you. I confeſsconfess the EpiſtleEpistle is large, but do but conſiderconsider your own conditions, and the preſentpresent diſpenſationsdispensations under which we are caſtcast, & then I ſuppoſesuppose you will not call it by the name of, a tedious EpiſtleEpistle.

Dear Friendsfriends, the following diſcourſediscourse
on CloſetCloset-closet prayer, I heartily recommend to your ſeriousserious peruſalperusal:. I have many reaſonsreasons to hope, that when you have once read it over, you will be more in love with CloſetCloset-closet prayer than ever, &and that you will ſetset a higher price upon CloſetCloset-closet prayer than ever, &and that you will make a better and fuller improvement of CloſetCloset-closet prayer, than ever yet you have done. ConſiderConsider what I ſaysay in my EpiſtleepistleEpistle to the Readerreader, &and labourlabor ſoso to manage this little TreatiſeTreatise,treatise that now I put into your hands, that God may be glorified, your own ſoulssouls edified, comfored &comforted, and encouraged in the wayesways of the Lord, and that you may be my Crowncrown and joy, in the great day of our Lord JeſusJesus (1Th 2:19-20)Jesus. So 1 TheſThes. 2. 19, 20. wiſhingwishing thatthat “ the good will of him that dwelt in the buſhbush,” (Deu 33:16) may abide upon you and yours for everforever, I take leave and reſtrest,

div.head: TO THE READER.
div.p: THetheThe EpiſtleepistleEpistle Dedicatorydedicatory being (occaſionallyoccasionally) ſoso large, I ſhallshall do little more than give thee the grounds and reaſonsreasons of ſendingsending forth this little piece into the Worldworld, eſpeciallyespecially in ſuchsuch a day as this is. NowNow, my reaſonsreasons are theſethese,:

FirſtFirst, BecauſebecauseBecause God by hisHis preſentpresent diſpenſationsdispensations calls more loudly for CloſetCloset-closet prayer now, than heHe hath done in thoſethose laſtlast twenty years that are now paſtpassedpast over our heads. See more of this in the 16.th Argumentargument for CloſetCloset-closet prayer, pag. 103, to p. 108.

Secondly, BecauſebecauseBecause I have ſeveralseveral reaſonsreasons to fear that many ChriſtiansChristians do not clearly nor fully underſtandunderstand the neceſſitynecessity, excellency, and uſefulneſsusefulness of this ſubjectsubject, and that many (O—oh, that I could not ſaysay any)— live in too great a neglect of this indiſpenſibleindispensableindispensible duty, and that more than a few, for want of light, erreerr in the very practice of it.

Thirdly, Forfor the refreſhingrefreshing, ſupportsupport, and encouragement of all thoſethose Churcheschurches of ChriſtChrist that walk in the fear of the Lord, and in the comforts of the Holy GhoſtGhost, &c. eſpeciallyespecially that particular Churchchurch to whom I ſtandstand related.

Fourthly, Toto preſervepreserve and keep up the power of Religionreligion and GodlineſsGodliness bothgodliness in mensmen’s houſeshouses, hearts, and lives. The power of Religionreligion and GodlineſsgodlinessGodliness lives, thrivesthrives, or dies as CloſetCloset-closet prayer lives, thrives, or dies. GodlineſsGodliness never riſesrises to a higher pitch than when men keep cloſeſtclosest to their CloſetsclosetsClosets, &c.

Fifthly, BecauſebecauseBecause Cloſetcloset Closet-prayer is a moſtmost ſovereignsovereign Remedyremedy, a moſtmost precious Antidoteantidote of GodsGod’s own preſcribingprescribing,prescribing againſtagainst the Plagueplague that now rageth in the midſtmidst of us, 1 Kings(1Ki 8.: 37, 38,- 39, &c).

Sixthly, BecauſebecauseBecause every man is that really, which he is ſecretlysecretly. Never tell me, how handſomlyhandsomelyhandsomly, how neatly, how bravely, this or that man acts his part before others; but tell me (, if thou canſtcanst), how he acts his part before God in his CloſetclosetCloset:; for the man is that certainly, that what he is ſecretlysecretly. I have not a little wondredwondered that ſoso many eminent Writerswriters ſhouldshould paſspass over this great and princely duty of CloſetCloset-closet prayer, either with a few brief touches, or elſeelse in a very great ſilencesilence. Eighthly and laſtlylastly, Thatthat favourfavor, that good acceptance, and fair quarter, that my other poor labourslabors have found, not onelyonly in this Nationnation, but in other Countryescountries alſoalso, hath put me upon putting pen to paper once more:. andAnd I hope thatthat “ the good will of him that dwelt in the buſhbush,” (Deu 33:16) will reſtrest upon this, as it hath (to the glory of free grace) reſtedrested upon my former endeaversendeavors. q.hi: But thouthou, when thou prayeſtprayest, enter into thy CloſetclosetCloset;, and when thou haſthast ſhutshut thy Doordoor, Praypray to thy Father which is in ſecretsecret,; and thy Father which ſeethseeth in ſecretsecret ſhallshall reward thee openly

div.p:
THeſeThese words of our SaviourSavior are plain, and to be taken litterallyliterally, and not Allegoricallyallegorically, for heHe ſpeakethspeaketh of ſhuttingshutting the Doordoor of the Chamberchamber. In this chapterchapter, there is a manifeſtmanifest oppoſitionopposition between
the PhariſeesPharisees praying in the Synagoguessynagogues and corners of the ſtreetsstreets, and others praying in ſecretsecret.

In the Texttext, you have a poſitivepositive Preceptprecept for every ChriſtianChristian to pray alone;: “ But thou, when thou prayeſtprayest:.” heHe ſaithsaith not, when (you) pray, but (thou), “ when (thou) prayeſtprayest, enter into thy cloſetcloset, &c. asAs” as ſpeakingspeaking not ſoso much of a joyntjoint duty of many praying together, as of a duty which each perſonperson is to do alone. The command in the Texttext ſendssends us as well to the CloſetclosetCloset as to the Churchchurch;. andAnd he is a hypocrite in grain that chooſeschooses the one and neglects the other; for thereby he tells the world he cares for neither, he makes conſcienceconscience of neither. He that puts on a religious habit abroad, to gain himſelfhimself a great Namename among men, and at the ſamesame time lives like an AtheiſtatheistAtheist at home, ſhallshall at the laſtlast be uncas'tuncased by God, and preſentedpresented before all the world for a Bellarm. de Sanctis, lib. 3. cap. 4. &c. moſtmost egrediousegregious hypocrite.

Bellarmine, and ſomesome others, turn the Texttext into an Allegoryallegory;. theyThey ſaysay
that in theſethese words there are two Allegoriesallegories. FirſtFirst, the Chamberchamber Doordoor is the SenſesenseSense: Shut the Door“shut thy door,,” that is (, ſaysay they), thy SenſesenseSense, leſtlest vain imaginations, and worldly thoughts diſtractdistract thy mind in praying. Secondly, Thethe Doordoor, ſaysay they, is our Mouthmouth.: Shut“shut thy Doordoor,,” that is, thy Lipslips (, ſaysay they), and let thy Prayerprayer be like the Prayerprayer of Hannah, conceived in thy mind, but not uttered with thy mouth. 'TisIt is'tis uſualusual with PapiſtspapistsPapists, and other monkiſhmonkish men, that lyelie in wait to deceive, to turn the bleſſedblessed Scriptures into a NoſenoseNose of Wax,wax under pretencepretense of Allegoriesallegories and MyſteriesmysteriesMysteries. Origen was a great admirer EuſebEuseb. Eccl. HiſtHist. Lib. 6. chap. 8. of Allegoriesallegories;. byBy the ſtrengthstrength of his parts and wanton wit, he turn'dturned moſtmost of the Scriptures into Allegoriesallegories; and by the juſtjust Judgementjudgment of God upon him, he fooliſhlyfoolishly underſtoodunderstood and abſurdlyabsurdly applied that Matth.ew 19.: 12. litterallyliterally:Litterally (“There be eunuchSomes, which have made themſelvesthemselves chaſteeunuchschaste for the Kingdomkingdom of Heaven)heaven’s sake,” and ſoso gelded himſelfhimself. And indeed he might as
well have pluck'tplucked out one of his eyes upon the ſamesame account, becauſebecause ChriſtChrist ſaithsaith,, “ It is betterbetter… to goenter tointo Heavenlife with one eye,, rather than having two eyes to be caſtcast into Hellhell fire Matth.” (Mat 18.: 99). In all Ages Hereticksages, heretics have commonly defended their HereſiesheresiesHeresies by tranſlatingtranslating of Scriptures into Allegoriesallegories. The ApoſtleapostleApostle ſpeaksspeaks of ſuchsuch, as, denying the ReſurrectionresurrectionResurrection of the body, turn all the teſtimoniestestimonies of the ReſurrectionresurrectionResurrection into an Allegoryallegory;, meaning thereby only the ſpiritualspiritual ReſurrectionresurrectionResurrection of the ſoulsoul from ſinsin;, of which ſortsort was HymeneusHymenaeus and Philetus, who deſtroyeddestroyed the faith of ſomesome, ſayingsaying “saying the ReſurrectionresurrectionResurrection was paſtpast already,” (2Ti 2 Tim. 2.: 17,- 1818). And are there not many among us that turn the whole HiſtoryhistoryHistory of the Bible into an Allegoryallegory;, and that turn ChriſtChrist, and Sinsin, and Deathdeath, and the Soulsoul, and Hellhell, and Heavenheaven, and all into an Allegoryallegory? Many have and many do miſerablymiserably pervert the Scriptures, by turning them into vain and groundleſsgroundless Allegoriesallegories. Some
wanton wits have expounded ParadiſeparadiseParadise Philo▪ Judaeus, and others of a later date. to be the Soulsoul, Manman to be the Mindmind, the Womanwoman to be the SenſesenseSense, the Serpentserpent to be Delightdelight, the Treetree of knowledge of good and evil to be WiſdomewisdomWisdom, and the reſtrest of the Treestrees to be the VertuesvirtuesVirtues and Endowmentsendowments of the Mindmind. O friends it! It is dangerous to bring in Allegories,allegories where the Scripture doth not clearly and plainly warrant them;, and to take thoſethose words Figuratively,figuratively which ſhouldshould be taken properly.

The word 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 ,ταμεῖον that is in the Texttext rendredrendered CloſetclosetCloset, hath only three moſtmost uſualusual ſignificationssignificationscommon meanings amongſtamongst Greek Authorsauthors. FirſtFirst, it may be taken for a ſecretsecret Chamber,chamber or cloſeclose and locked Parlourparlor.; Secondlysecondly, for a Safesafe or Cupbord,cupboard to lay Victualsfood in.; Thirdlythirdly, for a locked CheſtchestChest or Cupbord,cupboard wherein TreaſuretreasureTreasure uſuallyusually is reſervedreserved.

The beſtbest and moſtmost judicious Interpretersinterpreters that I have caſtcast mine eye upon, both of a former and later date, do all expound my Texttext of
Privateprivate Prayerprayer in retired places, and with them I cloſeclose:. And ſoso the main Doctrinedoctrine that I ſhallshall gather from the words is this:
div.q: ThatDoctrine: CloſetCloset-Prayer ( prayer or Private-Prayer)private prayer is an indiſpenſibleindispensableindispensible duty, that Doct. ChriſtChrist himſelfHimselfhimself hath laid upon all that are not willing to lyelie under the wofulwoeful brand of being Hypocriteshypocrites.
div.p: I beſeechbeseech you ſeriouſlyseriously to lay to heart theſethese five things.:

FirſtFirst, Ifif any Prayerprayer be a duty, then ſecretsecret Prayerprayer muſtmust needs be a duty; for ſecretsecret Prayerprayer is as much Prayerprayer as any other Prayerprayer is Prayerprayer; and ſecretsecret Prayerprayer prepares and fits the ſoulsoul for Family-Prayer,family prayer and for Publick-Prayerpublic prayer. Secret-Prayer prayer ſweetlysweetly enclines, &inclines and ſtronglystrongly diſpoſesdisposes a ChriſtianChristian to all other religious duties and ſervicesservices.
ErgoTherefo.re But,

Secondly secondly, Ifif Secretsecret Prayerprayer be not an indiſpenſibleindispensableindispensible duty that lyeslies upon thee, by what authority doth ConſcienceconscienceConscience ſoso upbraid thee, and ſoso accuſeaccuse thee, and ſoso condemn thee, and ſoso terrifieterrify thee, as it often doth
for the neglect of this duty? But,

Thirdly, Waswas it ever the way or method of God to promiſepromise again and again a reward, an open rewardreward, for that work or ſerviceservice which himſelfHe Himselfhimself never commanded? Surely Nonot. NowNow, to this duty of Secretsecret Prayerprayer, the Lord hath again and again promiſedpromised an open rewardreward (Mat 6:6, Matth. 6. 6. 1818). And thereforetherefore, without all peradventureany doubt, this is a duty incumbent upon all ChriſtiansChristians.

Fourthly, Ourour SaviourSavior in the Texttext takes it for granted, that every child of God, will be frequent in praying to hisHis heavenly Father,; and therefore he, He encourages them ſoso much the more in the work of Secretsecret Prayerprayer.. “ When you Praypray;”—as As if heHe had ſaidsaid, I know you can as well hear without earesears, and live without food, and fight without hands, and walk without feet, as you are able to live without Prayerprayer. And thereforetherefore, when you go to wait on God, or to give your heavenly Father a viſitvisit, Enter intoenter your
CloſetclosetCloset, and ſhutshut your doors, &cetc.

Fifthly, Ifif CloſetclosetCloset Prayerprayer be not an indiſpenſibleindispensableindispensible duty that ChriſtChrist hath laid upon all hisHis people, why doth Satan ſoso much oppoſeoppose it,? whyWhy doth he ſoso induſtriouſlyindustriously and ſoso unweariedly labourlabor to diſcouragediscourage ChriſtiansChristians in it, &and to take off ChriſtiansChristians from it? Certainly, Satan would never make ſuchsuch a fierce &and conſtantconstant war, as he doth upon private Prayer;prayer were it not a neceſſarynecessary duty, a reallreal duty, and a ſoulsoul-enriching duty. But more of this you will find in the following diſcourſediscourse; and thereforetherefore, let this touch ſufficesuffice for the preſentpresent, &c.

NowNow, theſethese five things do very clearly and evidently demonſtratedemonstrate thatthat to hold intercourse with God ſecretlysecretly and ſolitarilysolitarily to hold entercourſeentercourse with God is the undoubted duty of every ChriſtianChristian. But for a more full opening and confirmation of this great and important Pointpoint, I ſhallshall lay down theſethese Twentytwenty Argumentsarguments or ConſiderationsconsiderationsConsiderations, &c.

FirſtFirst, Thethe moſtmost eminent Saintssaints,
both in the Old and New TeſtamentTestament, have applied themſelvesthemselves to Private-Prayerprivate prayer. MoſesMoses was alone in the Mountmount with God forty dayesdays and fourtyforty nights, Exod(Exo. 34.: 2828). So Abraham fills his mouth with Arguments,arguments and reaſonsreasons the caſecase out alone with God in Prayer,prayer to prevent SodomsSodom’s deſolationdesolation and deſtructiondestruction, and never leaves off pleading and praying tilluntil he had brought God down from fifty to ten, ( Gen. 18.: 22-3232). andAnd in Gen.Genesis 21.: 33., youyouYou have Abraham again at his private prayers,: “ And Abraham planted a Grovegrove in Beer-ſhebashebaBeersheba, and called there on the name of the LordLORD, the everlaſtingeverlasting God..” Why did Abraham plant a Grovegrove, but that he might have a moſtmost private place to pray and pourepour out his ſoulsoul before the Lord in? So IſaacIsaac, Gen. 24. 63.: “ And IſaacIsaac went out to meditate in the field atat the eventideeventide” (Gen 24:63). The Hebrew word LaſuachLasuach,lasuach that is here rendredrendered Meditate,“meditate” ſignifiessignifies to pray as well as to meditate, and ſoso it is often uſedused. 'TisIt is'tis a comprehenſivecomprehensive word, that
takes in both Prayerprayer and Meditationmeditation. So you ſhallshall find Jacob at his private -prayer, Gen. 32. 24, 25, 26, 27, 28.: “ And Jacob was left alone:; and there wreſtledwrestled a man with him until the breaking of the dayday” (Gen 32:24-28). When Jacob was all alone, and in athe dark night, and when his joyntsjoints were out of joyntjoint, he ſoso wreſtleswrestles and weeps, and weeps and wreſtleswrestles in private Prayer,prayer that as a Princeprince at laſtlast he prevailesprevails with God. ( HoſHos. 12.: 3,- 44). So David, PſalPsal. 55. 16, 17.: “ As for me, I will call upon God:; and the LordLORD ſhallshall ſavesave me. Evening, and morning, and at noonnoon, will I pray, and cry aloud,: and he ſhallshall hear my voycevoice” (Psa 55:16-17).

So Daniel was three times a day in private prayer, Dan. 6. 10.: “ Now when Daniel knew that the Writingwriting was ſign'dsignedsign'd, he went into his houſehouse; and his Windowswindows being open in his Chamberchamber toward JeruſalemJerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetimeaforetime” (Dan 6:10). Daniel had accuſtomedaccustomed himſelfhimself to private prayer;. heHe went to his cloſetcloset, before he went to his publickpublic
employment and Statestate affairs:; and at his return to dinner, he turned firſtfirst into his Chamberchamber to ſerveserve his God, and refreſhrefresh his ſoulsoul, before he ſetsatset down to feaſtfeast his body:. andAnd at the end of the day, when he had diſpatchtdispatcheddispatcht his buſineſsbusiness with men, he made it his buſineſsbusiness to wait upon God in his Chamberchamber. So Jonah keeps up private prayer, when he was inin “ the Fiſhesfish’sFishes belly,,” yea, when he was inin “ the belly of Hellhell,” Jonah(Jon 2.: 1,- 2, &c). So we have EliasElijah at prayer under the Juniperjuniper Treetree, 1 Kings(1Ki 19.: 44). So Hannah, 1 Sam. 1. 13.: “ Now HannahHannah, ſheshe ſpeaksspakespeaks in her heart,; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heardheard” (1Sa 1:13). The very ſoulsoul of prayer lyeslies in the pouring out of the ſoulsoul before God, as Hannah did, ( verſvvers. 1515). Neither was RebecahRebekah a ſtrangerstranger to this duty, whowho, upon the Babesbabe’s ſtruglingstrugglingstrugling in her womb,, “ went to enquire of the Lord,LORD” ( Gen. 25.: 22. thatThat); that is, ſheshe went to ſomesome ſecretsecret place to pray, ſaithsaith Calvin, MuſculusMusculus, MercerMercerus, and others. So Saul is no ſoonersooner converted, but preſentlypresently
he falls upon private prayer, Acts 9. 11.: “ And the Lord ſaidsaid unto him, ariſeArisearise, and go into the ſtreetstreet which is called StraitStraight, and enquire in the houſehouse of Judas for one called SaulSaul, of TarſusTarsus: forfor, beholdbehold, he prayethprayeth” (Act 9:11). Though he was a ſtrictstrict PhariſeePharisee, yet he never prayed to purpoſepurpose before, nor neverever prayed in private before. div.p:

div.p:

div.label: f. The Issue of the Combat: Victory over the Angel
div.p:
Sixthly and laſtlylastly, Youyou have the iſſueissue of the CombatecombatCombat, and that is Victoryvictory over the Angel, ( verſvvers. 2828). The Angel was as freely and fully willing to be conquered by Jacob, as Jacob was willing to be conquerourconqueror. When
Loverslovers wreſtlewrestle, the ſtrongeſtstrongest is willing enough to take a fall of the weakeſtweakest; and ſoso 'twasit was here. Jacob by prayers and tears
did ſoso prince it with God, as that he carried the bleſſingblessing▪. JacobsJacob’s wreſtlingwrestling was by weeping, and his prevailing by praying. Prayers and tears are not only very pleaſingpleasing to God, but alſoalso very prevalent with God. div.label: Objection 1: We Have Much Business upon Our Hands

David was no ſluggiſhsluggish ChriſtianChristian, no ſloathfulslothfulsloathful ChriſtianChristian, no lazy ChriſtianChristian;. heHe uſedused to be in his cloſetcloset, when others were ſleepingsleeping in their beds. And I have read of TheodoſiusTheodosius the EmperouremperorEmperor, that after the variety Nicephorus of worldly imploymentsemployments relating to his civil affairesaffairs in the day timedaytime were over, how he was wont to conſecratetheconsecrate theconsecratethe greateſtgreatest part of the night to the ſtudyingstudying of the Scriptures and private prayer;, to which purpoſepurpose he had a Lamp,lamp ſoso artificiallyskillfully made, that it ſuppliedsupplied it ſelfselfitself with oyloil, so that ſoso he might no way be interrupted in his private retirements.

That Timetime ought to be redeemed, is a leſſonlesson that hathhas been taught by the very Heathensheathens themſelvesthemselves. 'TwasIt was'twas the ſayingsaying of Pittacus, one of the ſevenseven wiſewise men,, “ Know time, loſelose not a minute..” And ſoso TheophraſtusTheophrastus uſedused to ſaysay, That“ Time is of precious cost..” And ſoso Seneca,, “ Time is the only thing (,” ſaithsaith he), “ that we can innocently be covetous of; and yet there is nothing of which many are more laviſhlylavishly and profuſelyprofusely prodigal..” And
ChreſiusChrestus,Chresius a SophiſtersophisterSophister orof Byzantium in the time of Hadrianus the EmperouremperorEmperor, he was much given to Winewine; yet he alwayesalways counted time ſoso precious, that when he had miſſpentmisspent his time all the day, he would redeem it at night.

When Titus VeſpatianVespasianVespatian, who revenged ChriſtsChrist’sChrists blood on JeruſalemJerusalem, returned Victorvictor to Rome, remembringremembering Suetonius. one night as he ſatesatsate at ſuppersupper with his friends, that he had done no good that day, he uttered this memorable and praiſepraise-worthy ApothegmeApothegmpraiseworthy apophthegm,, “ AmiciAmici, diem perdidi,” ( My friends, I have loſtlost a dayday).
Chilo, one of the ſevenseven Sagessages, being asked what was the hardeſthardest thing in the world to be done, anſweredanswered,, “ To uſeuse and employ a mansman’s time well..”

Cato held, That that an account muſtmust be givengiven, not only of our labourlabor, but alſoalso of our leiſureleisure. And Aelian gives this teſtimonytestimony of the LacedemoniansLacedaemonians, Thatthat “ they were hugely covetous of their time, ſpendingspending it all about neceſſarynecessary things, and ſufferingsuffering

div.label: 6. Closet Prayer Is Either a Duty or It Is No Duty
div.p:
Sixthly, I anſweranswer, CloſetCloset prayer is either a duty, or 'tisit is no duty. Now that 'tisit is a duty, I have ſoso ſtronglystrongly proved, I ſuppoſesuppose, that no man nor devil, can fairly or honeſtlyhonestly deny it to be a duty. And thereforetherefore, why do men cry out of their great buſineſsbusiness? alaſsAlas duty! Duty muſtmust
be done, what ever whatever buſineſsbusiness is left undone; duty muſtmust. Duty muſtmust be done, or the man that neglects it, will be undone for everforever. 'TisIt is'tis a vainevain thing to object buſineſsbusiness, when a required duty is to be performed; andand, indeed, if the bare objecting of buſineſsbusiness, of much buſineſsbusiness, were enough to excuſeexcuse men from duty, I am afraid that there are but few duties of the GoſpelGospel,gospel but men would endeavourendeavor to evade, under a pretencepretense of buſineſsbusiness, of much buſineſsbusiness. He that pretends buſineſsbusiness to evade private prayer, will be as ready to pretend buſineſsbusiness to evade family prayer; and he that pretends buſineſsbusiness to evade family prayer, will be as ready to pretend buſineſsbusiness to evade publickpublic prayer.

have me excuſedexcused..” And,, “ I have married a Wifewife,,” ſaithsaith another,, “ and therefore I cannot comecome” (Luk 14:18-20). The things of the world and their carnal relatitionsrelations had taken up ſoso much room in their hearts and affections, that they had no ſtomackstomachstomack to heavensheaven’s dantiesdainties; and thereforetherefore, it is obſervableobservable, what ChriſtChrist adds at the end of the parable, He that hatethhateth “ not his Fatherfather, and Mothermother, and Wifewife, and Childrenchildren, and Brethrenbrethren, and SiſterssistersSisters, VerſVers. 26. yea, and his own Lifelife alſoalso,,” much more his Farmfarm and his Oxenoxen,, “ he cannot be my diſcipledisciple” (vdisciple.. 26).

div.p:

div.label: b. Take the Fittest Seasons and Opportunities for Closet Prayer
div.p:
My Secondsecond AdviſeadviceAdvise and counſelcounsel is this,: Take the fitteſtfittest ſeaſonsseasons and opportunities that poſſiblypossibly you can for CloſetCloset-closet prayer. Many take unfit ſeaſonsseasons for private prayer, which do more obſtructobstruct

FirſtFirst, Whenwhen the body is drowſiedrowsy Cant. 3. 1. and ſleepysleepy,; this is a very unfit ſeaſonseason for cloſetcloset-prayer prayer (Song 3:1). I have read a ſtorystory, how that one offered to give his horſehorse to his fellow upon condition he would but ſaysay the LordsLord’s Prayer, and think upon nothing but God;. theThe proffer was accepted, and he began,, “‘ Our Father, which art in Heavenheaven, Hallowed be thy name.name’ (Mat 6:9)… But I muſtmust have the bridle too (,” ſaidsaid he) no. “No, nor the HorſeHorse neither (horse either,” ſaidsaid the other), “ for thou haſthast loſtlost both already..” The application is eaſieeasy.

Certainly, the moſtmost free and lively ſeaſonsseasonseasons for CloſetCloset-closet prayer is the mornings, before a mansman’s ſpiritspirit be blunted or cooled, deadneddeadened, damped, or flatted by worldly buſineſſesbusinesses. div.p: FirſtFirst, A man may have Communioncommunion Sol. withwithWith God in ſorrowsorrow and tears, when he hath not Communioncommunion with God in joyjoy, delight; a (Psa 51:17). div.label: i. Look That the Glory of God Be Your Ultimate End
div.p: My Ninthninth Adviceadvice and CounſelcounselCounsel is this,: In all your CloſetclosetCloset- dutiesDuties, look that your ends be right,; look ChriſtusChristus opera noſtranostra, non tam actibus quam finibus penſatpensat. Zanch. that the Gloryglory of God be your ultimate end, the mark, the white, that you have in your eye. There is a great truth in that old ſayingsaying, (Quod non actibus, ſedsed finibus penſanturpensantur officia), That“ dutiesDuties are eſteemedesteemed not by their acts, but by their ends..”

LookLook, as the ſhiningshining Sunsun puts out the light of the fire;, ſoso the glory of God muſtmust conſumeconsume all other ends. There may be malum opus in bona materiamateria (a bad work in a good matter), as in JohuJehu's’s zeal. Two things make a good ChriſtianChristian, good actions, and good aims. And though a good aim doth not make a bad action good (, as in ƲzzahUzzah), yet a bad aim makes a good action bad (, as in Jehu), whoſewhose JuſticejusticeJustice was approved, but his Policypolicy puniſhedpunished. thy Lawlaw,; they have done nothing of all that thou haſthast commandedcommandedst them to dodo” (Jer 32:23). So Dan. 9. 13.“ All this evillevil is come upon us,: yet made we not our prayer before the LordLORD our GodGod” (Dan 9:13). IſaIsa. 58. 1, 2,- 3.; Zech.ariah 7.: 5,- 6. It was EphraimsEphraim’s folly, that he brought forth fruit unto himſelfhimself (Hos 10:1)himself. HoſHos. 10. 1. And it was the PhariſeesPharisees’Pharisees hypocriſiehypocrisy, that in all their duties and Mat. 6. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. ſervicesservices they looktlooked at the praiſepraise of men:. “ Verily,,” ſaithsaith ChriſtChrist, you“they have yourtheir reward;” a(Mat 6:1-5). A poor, a pitiful reward indeed.! Such men ſhallshall be ſuresure to fall ſhortshort of divine acceptance, and of a glorious recompencerecompense, that are not able to look above the praiſespraises of men. Duty)duty with a plauditeplaudit. As ever you would ask &and have, ſpeakspeak and ſpeedspeed, ſeekseek and find, look that the glory of the Lord be engraven upon all your cloſetcloset -duties.

He ſhallshall be ſuresure to ſpeedspeed beſtbest, whoſewhose heart is ſetset moſtmost upon glorifying of God in all his ſecretsecret retirements. When God Crownscrowns us, heHe doth but Crowncrown hisHis own gifts in us; and when we give God the Gloryglory of all we do, we do but give himHim the glory that is due unto hisHis Namename,; for 'tis heit is He, and heHe alone, that works all our works in us and for us. All CloſetclosetCloset Dutiesduties are good or bad, as the mark is at which the ſoulsoul aims. He that makes God the object of CloſetclosetCloset Prayerprayer, but not the end of CloſetclosetCloset Prayerprayer, doth but loſelose his Prayer,prayer and take pains to undoeundo himſelfhimself. Such prayers never reach the Earear of
God, nor delight the heart of God, nor ſhallshall ever be lodg'dlodged in the boſomebosom of God, that are not directed to the glory of God. The end muſtmust be as noble as the means, or elſeelse a man may be undone after all his doings. A mansman’s moſtmost glorious actions will at laſtlast be found to be but glorious ſinssins, if he hath made himſelfhimself, and not the glory of God, the end of thoſethose actions.
div.label: j. Offer All Your Closet Prayers in Christ’s Name, and in His Alone
div.p:
My Tenthtenth Adviceadvice and CounſelcounselCounsel is this,: Be ſuresure that you offer all your CloſetclosetCloset Prayersprayers in ChriſtsChrist’sChrists Namename, and in hisHis alone, John 14. 13, 14.“ And whatſoeverwhatsoever ye ſhallshall ask in my name, that will I do, that the fatherFather may be glorified in the ſonSonson. If ye ſhallshall ask any thing in my name, I will do itit” (Joh 14:13-14). John 15. 16.“ That whatſoeverwhatsoever ye ſhallshall ask of the fatherFather in my name, he may give it youyou” (Joh 15:16). John 16. 23, 24, 26.“ Verily, verily, I ſaysay unto you, whatſoeverwhatsoever ye ſhallshall ask the fatherFather in my name, he will give it you. Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye ſhallshall receive, that your joy may be full.… At that day ye ſhallshall ask in my name:
and I ſaysay notsay unto you, that I will pray the fatherFather for youyou” (Joh 16:23-24, 26). O Sirssirs,! thisThis is your Priviledgprivilege as well as your comfort, that you never deal with God but by a Mediatormediator. When you appear before God, JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist appears with you, and heHe appears for you; when you do invocare,, call on, pray, then heHe doth advocare;, call out to, advocate. whenWhen you put up your petitions, then heHe doth make interceſſionintercession for you. ChriſtChrist gives you a commiſſioncommission to put hisHis name upon all your requeſtsrequests; and whatſoeverwhatsoever prayer comes up with this name upon it, heHe will procure it an anſweranswer.

In the ſtatestate of innocencyinnocence, man might worſhipworship God without a Mediatormediator; but ſincesince ſinsin hath made ſoso wide a breach between God and Manman, God will accept of no worſhipworship from man, but what is offered up by the hand of a Mediatormediator:. Now this Mediatormediator is ChriſtChrist alone, 1 Tim. 2. 5.“ For there is one God, and one Mediatormediator between God &and men, the man ChriſtChrist JeſusJesus” (1Ti 2:5)Jesus. One Mediatormediator, not of Redemptionredemption only (, as the PapiſtspapistsPapists grant), but of
InterceſſionintercessionIntercession alſoalso, which they deny.

The PapiſtspapistsPapists make Saintssaints and Angelsangels co▪-mediators with ChriſtChrist; but in this, as in other things, they fight againſtagainst cleerclear Scripture -light. The ApoſtleapostleApostle plainly tells us, that the Officeoffice of InterceſſionintercessionIntercession pertaineth unto ChriſtChrist, as part of his MediationHis mediation (Heb 7: Heb. 7 25. And 'tis25); and it is certain, that we need no other MaſtermasterMaster of requeſtsrequests in Heaven,heaven but the man ChriſtChrist JeſusJesus;, whoWho being ſoso neernear to the Father, and ſoso dear to the Father, and ſoso much in with the Father, can doubtleſſedoubtless carry any thinganything with the Father, that makes for hisHis glory, and our good. This was typified in the Lawlaw:. The Highhigh PrieſtpriestPriest alone did enter into Ex. 28. 29. the Sanctuary,sanctuary and carry the names of the Childrenchildren of IſraelIsrael before the Lord, whil'ſtwhilstwhil'st the people ſtoodstood all without;. thisThis pointed out ChriſtsChrists MediationChrist’s mediation (Exo 28:29). In that Lev.iticus 16.: 1313-14, 14. youYouyou read of two things.: FirſtfirstFirst, of the cloud of IncenſeIncense,incense that covered the Mercymercy-Seatseat.;
Secondlysecondly, Ofof the blood of the Bullockbullock, that was ſprinkledsprinkled before the Mercymercy-Seatseat:. Now that blood typified Chriſt'sChrist’sChrist's ſatisfactionsatisfaction;, and the Cloudcloud of IncenſeincenseIncense hisHis InterceſſionintercessionIntercession.

Some of the learned think, that ChriſtChrist intercedes only by vertuevirtue of hisHis merits; others, that 'tisit is done only with hisHis mouth;. I conjecture it may be done both wayesways, the rather becauſebecause ChriſtChrist hath a tongue (, as alſoalso a whole body, but glorified), in Heavenheaven; and is it likely, that that mouth which pleaded ſoso much for us on earth, ſhouldshould be altogether ſilentsilent for us in Heavenheaven?

There is no coming to the Father, John 14. 6. but by the SonSon (Joh 14:6). ChriſtChrist is the true JacobsJacob’s Ladderladder, by which we muſtmust aſcendascend to Heavenheaven. JoſephJoseph,Joseph Gen. 43. you know, commanded his Brethren,brethren that as ever they looked for any good from him, or to ſeesee his face with joy, that they ſhouldshould be ſuresure to bring their Brotherbrother Benjamin along with them. O Sirssirs,!
asAs ever you would be prevalent with God, as ever you would have ſweetsweet, choice, and comfortable returns from Heavenheaven to all your CloſetCloset-closet prayers, be ſuresure that you bring your Elderelder Brotherbrother, the Lord JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist, in the arms of your faith,. beBe ſuresure that you treat and trade with God only in the name of the Lord JeſusJesus.

'TisIt is'tis a notable ſpeechspeech that Luther hath upon the 130.130th PſalmPsalm.: “ Often Dulce nomen ChriſtiChristi. and willingly (,” ſaithsaith he), “ do I inculcate this, that you ſhouldshould ſhutshut your eyes, and your ears, and ſaysay, you know no God out of ChriſtChrist, none but heHe that was in the lap of Mary, and ſuckedsucked her breaſtsbreasts:.” Dulce nomen Christi (Sweet is the name of Christ).
